sentences.text: Here's a pendulum one metre long, and beside it, a weight on a spring.
Two very different machines, and you can see them swinging in perfect step.
The pendulum takes about one second to swing across, and one second to swing back.
Now take two identical pendulums, and give one a wide swing and the other a narrow one.
You might expect the wide one to fall behind.
It doesn't: they keep the same beat.
So what rule makes things swing like this, and what sets the beat?
This part finds that rule, from the physics up.
Pendulums, alternating currents and waves all swing like this, and complex numbers turn out to be the natural language for all of them, from part two on.
The general theory of their equations comes next term.
Most of this part goes beyond the notes, which take the physics as given.
Here you build it from facts you already know.
First, the names.
Whatever swings, ex is how far it is from the middle.
It's signed: positive on one side, negative on the other.
Ex with one dot on top is its rate of change in time, the velocity.
Two dots means you take the rate of change again: that's the acceleration.
Now three quick questions, on tools this part will need.
A ten newton push on a two kilogram trolley.
What's its acceleration?
Five metres per second squared.
Force equals mass times acceleration, so you divide the force by the mass.
From here on, the acceleration is written ex double dot.
A right-angled triangle with a hypotenuse of ten, and an angle of thirty degrees.
How long is the side opposite that angle?
Ten times the sine of thirty degrees, which is five.
Last one: an arc of a circle with radius two and an angle of half a radian.
How long is it?
One.
Arc length is radius times angle, with the angle in radians.
All three get used in the next few minutes.
Start with the simplest thing that swings: a weight on a spring, lying on a smooth table, so gravity plays no part for now.
Pull the weight out, and the spring pulls back.
The further you pull, the harder it pulls.
Twice the stretch gives twice the pull: the pull is proportional to the stretch.
That's Hooke's law, from GCSE physics.
Now the sign.
Ex to the right is positive, and the pull points left.
Push the weight to the left, and you see both flip.
So the pull is minus the stiffness K, times ex.
The stiffness says how strong the spring is.
The minus sign means the pull always points back toward the middle.
But you want the motion, not the force.
Newton ties a force to an acceleration, and the acceleration is the position, differentiated twice.
So the move here is: name the force that pulls back, then let Newton turn it into an acceleration.
Force equals mass times acceleration.
The only force is the spring pulling back, so the mass M, times ex double dot, is minus K times ex.
Divide by the mass: ex double dot equals minus K over M, times ex.
That ratio, K over M, is the pull back per unit of stretch, for each kilogram it has to move.
Call it omega squared.
It's written as a square for a reason part two makes clear.
So ex double dot equals minus omega squared, times ex.
Out of context it looks abstract, but you can read it as: the acceleration always points back to the middle, and it grows with the distance.
Here's one for you.
Same spring, twice the mass.
Is the acceleration back toward the middle bigger or smaller, and by how much?
Pause the video if you want longer.
The pull depends only on the stretch, so it's the same as before.
But now it has twice the mass to move.
So the acceleration is half as big: minus K over two M, times ex.
A heavier weight on the same spring swings more slowly.
First, try it with numbers.
Say omega squared is four, and the weight is half a metre out.
Then the acceleration is minus four times a half: two metres per second squared, back toward the middle.
Now let it swing, out to half a metre on each side.
Keep your eye on the green velocity arrow and the red acceleration arrow.
Freeze it as it crosses the middle.
Here ex is zero, so the rule says there's no pull at all.
But the weight is moving at its fastest.
With nothing there to slow it down, it carries straight on past.
Now let it run out to the end of its swing, and freeze.
The weight is still, for an instant.
Is its acceleration zero there too?
Pause the video if you want longer.
You might expect so, since nothing is moving.
But the rule only looks at where the weight is, and here it's as far out as it ever gets.
So the pull is the largest it ever is: minus four times a half, minus two.
Being still and being free of any pull are two different things.
So now you can see why the weight never settles.
In the middle there's no pull, but it's moving too fast to stop.
At each end it stops, but that's where it's pulled hardest.
That's why it swings.
Now the pendulum: a weight called the bob, on a rod of length L, hung from a fixed point.
You measure its angle from the vertical, and call it theta for now.
Two forces act on the bob.
Gravity pulls it straight down with its weight: the mass M, times G, the strength of gravity.
And the rod pulls along itself, toward the pivot.
But the bob can only move along its arc, and the rod pulls at right angles to that.
So the rod can't speed the bob up, or slow it down.
So which part of gravity can?
The move here is: split gravity into a part along the rod and a part along the swing.
Only the part along the swing drives the motion.
Gravity points straight down.
The rod leans theta away from the vertical.
So gravity and the line of the rod are theta apart, too.
Now you draw gravity's arrow as the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle, with one side along the rod, and one along the swing.
The part along the swing is the side opposite theta: M times G, times the sine of theta, just like the triangle you saw at the start.
It points back toward the bottom, so the pull is minus M times G, times sine theta.
Watch gravity's pull as you change the angle.
At the bottom, theta is zero, and there's no pull at all.
Swing out to forty degrees, and gravity pulls with about sixty-four percent of the bob's weight.
Swing to the other side, and it flips, still pointing home.
Read it back: the further out the bob is, the harder gravity drags it home, but by the sine of the angle, not by the angle itself.
Now let Newton turn gravity's pull into an acceleration along the swing: the mass, times the acceleration along the swing, equals minus M times G, times sine theta.
Divide by the mass, and the acceleration along the swing is minus G, times sine theta.
The mass is gone.
Now a question for you.
Swap the bob for one twice as heavy.
Does the pendulum swing faster, slower, or the same?
Pause the video if you want longer.
The same.
Twice the mass means twice the weight, so the pull doubles too, and the two cancel.
The spring is different: its pull depends only on the stretch, which is why the heavier weight on the spring was slower.
There's one snag left.
Newton counts the distance the bob travels, but you're describing the pendulum by its angle.
The arc turns one into the other.
The bob moves on a circle of radius L, so its distance along the arc is L times theta, with theta in radians.
The length L is fixed, so differentiate twice: the acceleration along the arc is L times theta double dot.
Put that in: the length L, times theta double dot, equals minus G, times sine theta.
Divide by the length L: theta double dot equals minus G over L, times sine theta.
Now read it back, next to the spring's rule.
It's almost the same, but with the sine of theta where theta should be.
And that sine makes it much harder: this equation has no answer in any functions you know.
So here's the last move: for small swings, trade sine theta for theta.
To see why that's fair, you can compare two lengths on the same picture.
The bob's sideways reach is L times sine theta, the side opposite the angle.
Its distance along the arc is L times theta.
For a small swing, the arc is nearly straight, so the two almost agree.
How good is that trade, would you guess?
At a tenth of a radian, the sine is point zero nine nine eight: two tenths of a percent short.
At ten degrees, it's half a percent short.
At thirty degrees, four and a half percent.
At sixty degrees, the sine is seventeen percent short, and the trade starts to fail.
So for small swings, theta double dot is about minus G over L, times theta.
That's the spring's rule exactly, with omega squared equal to G over L.
So omega is the square root of G over L.
Read it back: a longer pendulum is pulled back more gently, for each radian of swing.
For the one metre pendulum, omega squared is nine point eight one, so omega is about three point one three per second.
What that does to its beat is part two's story.
One honest warning.
At big angles, gravity really pulls with the sine of theta, and that is weaker than the rule, which uses theta itself.
So for big swings the rule is only an approximation, and part two shows what that costs.
For small swings, though, you now have the rule.
So here are two very different machines, obeying one rule: ex double dot equals minus omega squared, times ex.
For the spring, omega squared is K over M.
For the pendulum, it's G over L.
From now on, whatever swings, you call its displacement ex, even when it's an angle.
Anything pulled back in proportion to how far out it is obeys this rule.
Its motion has a name: simple harmonic motion.
Time for a recap.
First move: name the force that pulls back, then use Newton to turn it into an acceleration.
Second: split gravity along the rod and along the swing.
Only the swing part drives the bob.
Third: for small swings, trade sine theta for theta, because the arc and the reach almost agree.
And four facts you need to keep: Newton's law, Hooke's law, G is nine point eight one metres per second squared, and arc length is radius times angle.
Next time: which motion obeys this rule?
You need a function that comes back as minus omega squared times itself after two derivatives.
The answer is the shadow of an arrow that turns in a circle.
